newsitem.title: USA: Coors posts higher profits on Molson royalty payment.
newsitem.headline: Coors posts higher profits on Molson royalty payment.

text.p: Adolph Coors Co. posted higher third-quarter profits Thursday, but the gain was the result of a special payment from Molson Breweries related to royalties from the sales of Coors beer in Canada.
The Colorado brewer said its net income for the 13 weeks ended Sept. 29 rose to $18.7 million, or 49 cents a share, from $16.5 million, or 43 cents a share.
However, the increase was primarily due to an after-tax credit of $4.1 million, or 11 cents share, related to a Molson payment of $4.8 million for under-paid royalties, Coors said.
The company, the third-largest brewer in the United States, also said $1.9 million of income resulted from the continuing effects of changes in its payroll practices.
Excluding special items, Coors said its third-quarter profits slipped to $14.6 million, or 38 cents a share.
Coors, which is based in Golden, Colo., said its sales for the period slipped to $453.5 million from $455.4 million, despite higher prices for its beer and other malt beverages.
It said unit sales volume fell 3.3 percent to 5.36 million barrels from 5.54 million barrels in 1995.
The company said the decline was the result of inventory build-ups by its distributors for the Fourth of July holiday in the second quarter, rather than in the third quarter like last year.
It also said sales were hurt by greater than usual reductions in distributors' inventories at the end of the summer.
Coors also said it had reached an interim agreement with Molson Breweries for Molson to continue to brew and market Coors products in Canada until at least June 30, 1997.
The company estimated that it will receive at least an additional $10 million of pretax income from Molson during that period.

The agreement follows an Oct. 18 ruling by an arbitration panel in Toronto that Molson relinquished all of its rights to brew and distribute Coors products in 1993 when Miller Brewing Co. purchased an ownership interest in the Canadian brewer.
The $4.8 million payment by Molson for under-paid royalties was a result of the panel's ruling.
Coors said it was pleased with the arbitration ruling but could not predict its full financial impact.
"Although Coors believes that the amount of damages is significant, it cannot be determined until the next phase of arbitration is completed during 1997," the company said in a statement.
Coors said the ruling returned all Canadian rights to Coors products back to the company and said it will look at a number of options for its future in Canada.
"Our future business opportunities in Canada could provide significantly greater financial returns than we would have received under the terminated license arrangement," Coors said.

For the first nine months of the year, Coors said its net income grew 6.6 percent to $39.5 million, or $1.04 a share, from $37.0 million, or 97 cents a share, as sales expanded by 5 percent to $1.32 billion from $1.26 billion.
It said year-to-date sales volume increased 0.6 percent to 15.42 million barrels.

Coors said that in addition to the third-quarter special credit, its nine-months results also included a second-quarter after-tax charge of $3.2 million, or 8 cents a share, related to the Molson legal proceedings and to restructuring of the company's engineering and construction operations.
Without special charges, Coors said, year-to-date profits grew 4.1 percent to $38.5 million, or $1.01 per share.
Coors stock lost 62.5 cents to $17.875 in early trading on the Nasdaq market.
